lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Gold mining can be dangerous, but most accidents are preventable. In artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) across Africa, thousands of miners are injured or killed each year due to collapses, falls, chemical exposure, and poor equipment handling. In Tanzania alone, it is estimated that over 30% of mining accidents are fatal. These are not just statistics; they are fathers, mothers, and children. Safety is not optionalâit is the foundation of a sustainable livelihood.

Why does safety matter? First, your life and health are irreplaceable. A broken leg from a fall can keep you out of work for months. Second, a safe mine is a productive mine. When you follow safety rules, you spend less time treating injuries and more time extracting gold. Third, safe practices protect your community. Mercury and cyanide can poison water sources, harming families and livestock downstream.

In this module, you will learn the essential safety practices for every stage of gold mining: from choosing the right tools to handling chemicals and responding to emergencies. We focus on practical, low-cost solutions that you can apply immediately, even with limited resources. You do not need expensive gear to be safeâyou need knowledge and discipline.

Remember: no gold is worth your life. Always prioritize safety over speed. By the end of this module, you will be able to identify hazards, use protective equipment, and follow procedures that keep you and your team alive and healthy.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
Using the right tools and materials is your first line of defense against accidents. In artisanal gold mining, many injuries come from makeshift equipment. Invest in these basics: a hard hat (or at least a sturdy helmet) to protect your head from falling rocks; steel-toed boots to prevent foot injuries; and heavy-duty gloves to protect your hands from sharp rocks and chemicals. If you cannot afford new gear, look for second-hand industrial equipment at local markets or ask NGOs for donations.

For underground work, you need proper lighting. A headlamp with rechargeable batteries (like those used by cyclists) is better than a handheld torch because it keeps your hands free. Always carry a spare battery or a backup light. Ventilation is critical: without proper airflow, you can suffocate or be exposed to toxic gases. Use a hand-cranked or solar-powered fan if electricity is unavailable. Never enter a shaft without testing the air firstâlower a lit candle; if it goes out, the air lacks oxygen.

For chemical handling, you need personal protective equipment (PPE): a respirator mask (not just a cloth) for mercury vapors, chemical-resistant gloves, and goggles. Store chemicals in sealed containers away from food and water. For mercury, use a retortâa simple device that captures mercury vapor. Retorts can be made locally from metal pipes and cost less than $20. For cyanide, never use it without training; it is deadly.

Other essentials: a first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and pain relievers; a rope for emergency escape; and a whistle to signal for help. Keep tools sharp and well-maintainedâa dull pickaxe requires more force and can slip. Replace worn ropes and broken handles immediately. Remember, good tools are an investment in your safety and productivity.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps to work safely in gold mining. Step 1: Conduct a risk assessment before starting work. Walk around the site and look for loose rocks, unstable ground, poor ventilation, and chemical spills. Write down hazards and fix them before anyone enters. Step 2: Put on your PPE. This includes hard hat, boots, gloves, goggles, and respirator if needed. Check that your gear is in good conditionâno cracks in the helmet, no holes in gloves.

Step 3: Secure the work area. For underground mining, install roof supports (timber or rock bolts) every 1-2 meters. Never work under an unsupported roof. For open pits, build a barrier at the edge to prevent falls. Use ropes and harnesses if working at height. Step 4: Ensure proper ventilation. Open all vents and use a fan if necessary. Test the air with a canary or a gas detector. If you feel dizzy or short of breath, evacuate immediately.

Step 5: Handle chemicals safely. If using mercury, always work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Use a retort to capture vapors. Never heat mercury indoors. For cyanide, wear full PPE and have an antidote kit nearby. Store chemicals in labeled, sealed containers. Step 6: Communicate. Use a buddy systemânever work alone. Establish hand signals or radios for emergencies. Set a check-in schedule.

Step 7: Respond to emergencies. If a collapse occurs, turn off equipment, evacuate, and call for help. If someone is injured, apply first aid and transport them to a clinic. For chemical exposure, move to fresh air, remove contaminated clothing, and rinse with water. Step 8: Clean up. After work, wash hands and face, change clothes, and shower. Dispose of chemical waste properlyânever pour into rivers. Following these steps reduces accidents by up to 80%.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Ignoring PPE because it is uncomfortable. Fix: Choose gear that fits well. Break in boots before long shifts. If respirators are hot, take short breaks in fresh air. Remember, discomfort is better than injury.

Mistake 2: Working alone. Fix: Always use a buddy system. If you must work alone, tell someone your location and expected return time. Carry a whistle or phone.

Mistake 3: Poor ventilation in underground mines. Fix: Never rely on natural airflow alone. Install a ventilation fan or use a chimney effect with a vertical shaft. Test air quality with a candle or gas meter before entering.

Mistake 4: Using mercury without a retort. Fix: Build or buy a retort. If unavailable, work outdoors and stay upwind. Never heat mercury in a closed room. Store mercury in a sealed container under water.

Mistake 5: Not securing tunnel roofs. Fix: Install supports every 1-2 meters. Use timber or rock bolts. Inspect roofs daily for cracks or loose rocks. Never enter a tunnel that looks unstable.

Mistake 6: Skipping first aid training. Fix: Take a basic first aid course. Learn to treat cuts, fractures, and chemical burns. Keep a well-stocked kit and check expiry dates.

Mistake 7: Ignoring health symptoms. Fix: If you feel dizzy, nauseous, or have headaches, leave the mine. These can be signs of gas exposure or exhaustion. Rest and seek medical help.

Mistake 8: Improper chemical storage. Fix: Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated shed away from living areas. Label all containers. Never store chemicals in food or drink bottles.

Mistake 9: Using damaged tools. Fix: Inspect tools daily. Replace worn ropes, cracked handles, and dull drill bits. A broken tool can cause serious injury.

Mistake 10: Rushing. Fix: Slow down. Most accidents happen when miners rush to meet targets. Take regular breaks and stay focused. No gold is worth a life.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Best practices go beyond basic safetyâthey create a culture of care. Start with daily safety meetings. Spend 5 minutes each morning discussing hazards and assigning tasks. Use a checklist to ensure all safety measures are in place. Encourage workers to report near-misses without fear of punishment. This helps identify risks before they cause harm.

Invest in training. Teach all workers how to use PPE, handle chemicals, and respond to emergencies. Invite local health workers to give first aid demonstrations. Practice emergency drills monthly: simulate a collapse, fire, or chemical spill. Ensure everyone knows escape routes and assembly points.

Maintain equipment. Schedule regular maintenance for pumps, fans, and vehicles. Keep a log of repairs. Replace worn parts immediately. For underground mines, monitor ground stability with crack meters or simple visual inspections. Install rock bolts and mesh in high-risk areas.

Manage chemicals responsibly. Use mercury only in a retort and recycle it. Never use cyanide without proper training and permits. Store chemicals in a secure, ventilated area. Have spill kits ready: sand, sawdust, and neutralizing agents. Dispose of waste at approved facilitiesânever in rivers or soil.

Promote health and hygiene. Provide clean drinking water and sanitation facilities. Encourage workers to wash hands before eating. Offer vaccinations for tetanus and hepatitis. Support workers' mental healthâmining can be stressful. Create a supportive environment.

Engage the community. Inform nearby villages about your operations and potential risks. Share safety information. Work with local authorities to enforce safety regulations. Join or form a miners' association to share best practices and advocate for safer conditions.

Finally, lead by example. Owners and supervisors must follow the same safety rules. When leaders prioritize safety, workers do too. Remember, safety is not a costâit is an investment that saves lives and improves productivity.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
This exercise will help you apply safety practices in a simulated mining environment. You will need: a hard hat, gloves, boots, goggles, a respirator (if available), a first aid kit, a rope, a whistle, and a candle or gas detector. Work in a team of at least three people.

Step 1: Risk Assessment. Choose a small area (e.g., a backyard or open field) and pretend it is a mine site. Walk around and identify at least five hazards (e.g., loose rocks, holes, sharp objects). Write them down and discuss how to fix each one.

Step 2: PPE Drill. Put on all your PPE correctly. Have a partner check your gear: Is your hard hat secure? Are your gloves on properly? Adjust as needed. Time yourselfâaim to be fully geared in under 2 minutes.

Step 3: Ventilation Test. In a confined space (like a shed with closed windows), light a candle. Observe how long it burns. Then open a window or use a fan and test again. Discuss why ventilation matters.

Step 4: Emergency Response. Simulate a tunnel collapse. One person plays the injured miner, another the rescuer, and the third the caller. Practice using the rope to rescue someone from a pit. Use the whistle to signal for help. Apply first aid (e.g., bandage a fake wound).

Step 5: Chemical Safety. Set up a mock mercury station. Use a retort (or a sealed container) to demonstrate safe handling. Practice storing chemicals in labeled containers. Discuss what to do in a spill.

Step 6: Debrief. After the exercise, gather your team and discuss what went well and what needs improvement. Create an action plan for your real mining site. Repeat this exercise monthly to keep skills sharp.

By completing this exercise, you will be better prepared to handle real emergencies and protect yourself and your colleagues.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Safety in Artisan Gold Mining

This practical reference is built for artisan gold miners, small-scale operators, and the community health workers and extension officers who support them across Africa. It assumes you already understand the basic steps of digging, crushing, washing, panning, and amalgamating. Here we focus on the practical, field-tested safety measures that protect your life, your workers, your community, and your licence to operate. Safety is not a cost centre. It is a business continuity strategy. A mine that kills or poisons its workers does not produce gold for long.

Artisan gold mining in Africa is a livelihood for millions, from Ghana and Tanzania to Zimbabwe, Mali, Burkina Faso, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. It generates income, but it also exposes miners to mercury poisoning, tunnel collapse, dust-related lung disease, chemical burns, and physical injury. The World Health Organization estimates that artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) is the largest single source of mercury exposure for humans globally, with an estimated 10 to 20 million miners involved, including women and children. The practical reference below gives you the numbers, the tools, and the checklists you need to reduce harm without shutting down production.

The diagram above contrasts the two operating modes you will see on almost every artisanal site in Africa. The unsafe side is cheaper today and more expensive tomorrow. The safe side costs a little more in time and equipment but keeps your crew alive, your community healthy, and your operation legal under the Minamata Convention, which most African gold-producing countries have now ratified.

Table 1: Mercury Exposure and Health Effects in ASGM

Exposure Route At-Risk Group Health Effect Prevention
Inhalation of mercury vapour during burning Miners, women, children near amalgam burning Tremors, memory loss, kidney damage, respiratory failure Use retort; burn outdoors away from homes; wear respirator
Skin contact with liquid mercury Miners handling amalgam bare-handed Dermatitis, absorption into bloodstream Nitrile gloves; never touch mercury with bare hands
Contaminated water and fish Downstream communities, pregnant women Methylmercury poisoning; neurological damage in fetuses Contain tailings; never discharge mercury into rivers
Contaminated soil and dust Children playing on tailings; food crops Chronic low-dose poisoning; developmental delays Fence tailings; wash hands; keep children away

Source: World Health Organization, Mercury and health fact sheet (2023); UNEP, Global Mercury Assessment (2018).

Table 2: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for Artisan Gold Mining

Task Required PPE Estimated Cost (USD) Local Source in Africa
Digging and tunnelling Hard hat, steel-toe boots, dust mask, headlamp 25â40 Hardware stores, mining supply shops (Accra, Dar es Salaam, Harare)
Crushing and grinding Respirator (N95 or better), goggles, gloves, ear protection 20â35 Pharmacies, industrial safety suppliers
Panning and washing Waterproof boots, gloves, long sleeves 10â20 Local markets, agricultural supply stores
Amalgamation and burning Nitrile gloves, respirator, goggles, apron, retort 30â60 (retort extra) NGOs, government mining offices, mercury-free gold programmes
Hauling and transport Boots, gloves, reflective vest 15â25 Local markets, safety suppliers

Source: Adapted from the International Labour Organization, Safety and health in small-scale surface mines (2001), and Pact, Mercury-Free Gold: A Practical Guide for Artisanal Miners (2020).

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: MERCURY AND TUNNEL COLLAPSE

Never burn mercury amalgam indoors, near food, or near children. Mercury vapour is odourless, invisible, and highly toxic. A single unprotected burn can cause permanent brain and kidney damage. Always use a retort and burn outdoors, upwind, at least 50 metres from homes. Equally, never enter an unsupported tunnel deeper than 5 metres. In 2019, a collapse in a Zimbabwean artisanal gold mine killed at least 20 miners. Support every tunnel with timber or rock bolts, and always work with a partner and a second exit. If you feel dizzy, short of breath, or see dust that hangs in the air, get out immediately.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Ventilate before you enter. Test the air with a canary or gas monitor. If a flame won't stay lit, there is not enough oxygen. Do not enter.
  2. Support every tunnel. Use timber sets or rock bolts every 1â1.5 metres. Never work under loose rock.
  3. Wear your PPE. Hard hat, boots, gloves, respirator, goggles. No exceptions, even for a quick job.
  4. Handle mercury safely. Use a retort, gloves, and a tray. Never touch mercury with bare hands. Never burn indoors.
  5. Control dust. Wet the ore before crushing. Wear a respirator. Dust causes silicosis and tuberculosis.
  6. Keep children away. No child under 18 should be on the mining site, especially near pits, mercury, or machinery.
  7. Have an emergency plan. Two exits, a buddy system, a first-aid kit, and a phone or whistle signal.
  8. Report and record. Log every incident, near-miss, and health complaint. Use the data to fix the hazard, not to blame the worker.

Further Reading

  • WHO â Mercury and Health Fact Sheet (free, official, regularly updated)
  • UNEP Global Mercury Partnership â Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (free guidance and national action plan templates)
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Small-Scale Surface Mines (free code of practice, Africa-relevant)
  • Pact â Mercury-Free Gold: A Practical Guide for Artisanal Miners (free, field-tested in Africa)
  • Minamata Convention on Mercury â Official Texts and Guidance (free, legally binding for ratifying African states)

Business-first takeaway: Safe mines attract better financing, sell to formal buyers, and avoid the fines, closures, and medical costs that destroy margins. Train your crew on this reference, keep the checklist posted at the pit head, and budget for PPE as a line item, not an afterthought. In African ASGM, the operators who survive and scale are the ones who treat safety as an asset, not a burden.

quiz.q: What is the primary reason safety matters in gold mining?
options: B) To protect lives and health
quiz.explanation: Safety is fundamentally about preserving human life and health, which is more important than any production goal.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a basic PPE for gold mining?
quiz.explanation: Sunglasses do not provide protection against mining hazards; they are not considered PPE for this context.

quiz.q: Why is a retort important when using mercury?
options: A) It makes mercury more reactive
B) It captures mercury vapor to prevent inhalation
D) It cools the mercury quickly
quiz.explanation: A retort captures toxic mercury vapors, protecting miners from poisoning.

quiz.q: What should you do before entering an underground mine?
options: A) Test the air with a candle
quiz.explanation: Testing the air with a candle helps detect low oxygen levels; if the candle goes out, the air is unsafe.

quiz.q: How often should roof supports be installed in a tunnel?
quiz.explanation: Frequent supports (every 1-2 meters) are necessary to prevent collapses.

quiz.q: What is the buddy system?
options: A) Working alone to save money
B) Always working with at least one other person
C) Sharing tools with a friend
quiz.explanation: The buddy system ensures that someone is always available to help in an emergency.

quiz.q: Which chemical is deadly and requires special training?
quiz.explanation: Cyanide is highly toxic and should only be used by trained professionals with proper permits.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake regarding PPE?
options: B) Ignoring it because it is uncomfortable
quiz.explanation: Miners often skip PPE due to discomfort, but this leads to preventable injuries.

quiz.q: How can you improve ventilation in a mine?
options: B) Use a fan or open vents
quiz.explanation: Proper ventilation requires airflow, which can be achieved with fans or open vents.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy in a mine?
quiz.explanation: Dizziness can indicate gas exposure or lack of oxygen; evacuate to fresh air immediately.

quiz.q: Why is it important to store chemicals properly?
options: B) To avoid contamination and poisoning
D) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Improper storage can lead to leaks, fires, and poisoning of people and the environment.

quiz.q: What is a near-miss?
options: A) An accident that causes injury
B) An unplanned event that did not cause harm
quiz.explanation: A near-miss is an incident that could have caused harm but didn't; reporting them helps prevent future accidents.

quiz.q: How often should emergency drills be conducted?
options: D) Only when new workers arrive
quiz.explanation: Monthly drills keep emergency response skills sharp and ensure everyone knows what to do.

quiz.q: What is the first step in a risk assessment?
options: B) Walk around and identify hazards
quiz.explanation: Identifying hazards is the first step to fixing them and preventing accidents.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a stable tunnel roof?
options: C) No visible cracks or movement
quiz.explanation: A stable roof shows no signs of cracking or falling rocks; any such signs indicate danger.

quiz.q: What should you do with chemical waste?
options: A) Pour it into a river
B) Bury it in your backyard
C) Dispose of it at approved facilities
D) Burn it in the open
quiz.explanation: Proper disposal prevents environmental contamination and protects community health.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to work alone?
options: B) No one can help if you get injured
quiz.explanation: Working alone means no immediate assistance in case of an accident, increasing the risk of fatality.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to test air quality underground?
quiz.explanation: A candle's flame will go out if oxygen is low, indicating unsafe air.

quiz.q: What should be included in a first aid kit?
quiz.explanation: A first aid kit should contain supplies to treat common injuries like cuts and burns.

quiz.q: How can you prevent falls in an open pit?
options: B) Build a barrier at the edge
quiz.explanation: Barriers or ropes at the edge prevent accidental falls into the pit.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a safety meeting?
options: B) To discuss hazards and plan safety measures
quiz.explanation: Daily safety meetings ensure everyone is aware of risks and how to mitigate them.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for chemical handling?
options: B) Using a retort for mercury
C) Storing chemicals in drink bottles
quiz.explanation: Using a retort for mercury is a best practice that captures toxic vapors.

quiz.q: What should you do if a colleague is injured?
options: B) Apply first aid and call for help
quiz.explanation: Applying first aid and seeking professional help can save a life.

quiz.q: Why is it important to maintain tools?
options: A) To make them look new
B) To prevent accidents from broken tools
quiz.explanation: Well-maintained tools are less likely to break and cause injuries.

quiz.q: What is a retort made of?
quiz.explanation: Retorts can be made from metal pipes and are used to capture mercury vapor.

quiz.q: How can you protect your community from mining hazards?
options: B) Inform them about risks and safety measures
quiz.explanation: Transparency and education help the community stay safe and support your operations.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if you see a loose rock in a tunnel?
options: B) Remove it carefully or install support
quiz.explanation: Loose rocks can fall and cause injury; they must be secured or removed.

quiz.q: What does PPE stand for?
quiz.explanation: PPE refers to gear like helmets, gloves, and respirators that protect the wearer.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wash hands after work?
quiz.explanation: Washing removes toxic chemicals that can be ingested with food.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for storing mercury?
options: B) Under a layer of water in a sealed container
quiz.explanation: Storing mercury under water in a sealed container prevents vapor release.
